title: What Is MCP? Model Context Protocol in Plain Language
h1: What is MCP (Model Context Protocol), and what does it change for a firm
desc: MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard that lets AI assistants reach a firm's tools and data. How a connector works, and what to connect first.
lead: MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard Anthropic introduced in November 2024. It lets an AI assistant connect to other tools and data, such as email, calendars, files, databases and business software. For a firm, that means the assistant can read and act on the firm's own information, instead of only what someone pastes into the chat.
short: MCP is an open standard, introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, for connecting AI assistants to tools and data.
A connector (an MCP server) sits between the assistant and one tool, and decides what the assistant can see and do there.
Permissions matter more than the technology. Start with read access, and have a person approve anything sent to a client.
Connect first the tool the team copies from most. That's usually email, calendar, a shared drive or the main client database.

sections.h2: What is MCP, in plain language?
body: MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. It's an agreed set of rules for how an AI assistant asks another piece of software for information, and how that software answers. Anthropic released it as an open standard in November 2024, and other AI companies and software makers have since adopted it.

Think of a standard plug. Before everyone agrees on one, each device needs its own adapter. Once the plug is agreed, anything built to it fits any socket built to it. MCP does that job between AI assistants and the tools a firm already uses.

Without a connection, an assistant knows what it was trained on and whatever someone types into the conversation. That's all. Connect it, and it can look things up in the firm's records at the moment the question is asked.

sections.h2: What does MCP change for a firm's AI assistant?
body: Watch someone use an assistant today and most of the effort goes into feeding it. They open the client file, copy the relevant part, paste it in, ask the question, then copy the answer back into another tool. The assistant is capable enough. It just can't see anything.
Connected to the firm's tools, the same assistant can do things like these:
Find the latest thread with a client in the inbox, without anyone pasting it in.
Check the calendar before drafting a reply that suggests a meeting time.
Read a record in the client or candidate database and answer a question about it.
Prepare a document from a template in the shared drive and file it in the right folder.
Draft a reply to a client and leave it waiting in the drafts folder.
None of this makes the assistant smarter. It gets access to what the team already holds, which was usually the missing piece.

sections.h2: How does an MCP connector work?
body: A connector, also called an MCP server, is a small program that sits between the assistant and one tool. It tells the assistant what it's allowed to do there, such as search messages, read a record or create a draft. When the assistant needs something, it asks the connector, which fetches it from the tool and hands it back.
Here's what happens, step by step:
A team member asks a question that needs outside information.
The assistant checks which connectors are available and what each one offers.
It calls the right action, say a search in the recruiting database.
The connector checks its permissions, then runs the request in the tool.
The result comes back, and the assistant uses it in its answer and can say where it came from.

Plenty of common tools already have ready connectors, and Claude keeps a directory of them. If a tool has none, a connector can be built against the tool's API, the interface the software offers to other programs.

sections.h2: What do permissions mean, and why do they matter?
body: A connector acts with the access it's given, which is usually the access of whoever signs in. If that person can open every client file, so can the assistant. If the connector is allowed to send email, the assistant can send email. Of all the decisions in the setup, this one matters most.

It helps to separate three levels. Read access lets the assistant look things up. Draft access lets it prepare messages and documents without sending them. Write or send access lets it change records or send things on the firm's behalf.

Loose Ends starts with read access and adds draft access where a routine needs it. A person approves anything that goes to a client. Most assistants also ask for confirmation before an action that changes something, and that setting should stay on. Before connecting anything, decide which data the firm is comfortable letting the assistant see at all, and leave sensitive folders out.

sections.h2: What should a firm connect first?
body: Start with the tool the team copies from most. There's an easy way to find it. Watch an ordinary week and note every time someone opens a tool only to copy text into the assistant or into another tool. Whichever tool keeps coming up goes first.
In most firms the order runs roughly like this:
Email and calendar, because answering, confirming and scheduling touch almost every role.
The shared drive or document store, so the assistant can work from the firm's templates, past proposals and notes.
The main client, case or candidate database, where the questions that matter most get answered.
Team chat such as Slack, where decisions get made in conversation and are never written down anywhere else.
One connection the team trusts beats several it doesn't. Add the next once people rely on the first.

sections.h2: How does Loose Ends set up MCP connections?
body: The studio connects Claude and other assistants to the tools a firm already runs on: email, calendar, Slack, spreadsheets and databases, Loxo, BrightHire, Shopify, Etsy and Substack. It uses a ready Claude connector where one exists and builds a custom API integration where none does. Each connection gets the narrowest access that does the job, and it's tested on real questions from the team before handover.
At handover, every routine that uses a connection has a named owner inside the firm. The team learns what the assistant can and can't reach. Code, accounts and access belong to the firm.
To find out where a connection would save the most copying and retyping, ask Loose Ends for the free one-page review of where the firm loses time. No call is needed.

faq.q: Is MCP only for Claude?
faq.a: No. Anthropic released MCP as an open standard, and other AI assistants and tools have adopted it. A connector built to the standard works with any assistant that supports it.

faq.q: Does connecting an assistant to our tools mean it can send email on its own?
faq.a: Only if the connector has that permission. A careful setup starts with read and draft access, and a person approves anything before it goes to a client.

faq.q: What if the tool we use has no MCP connector?
faq.a: If it has an API, a connector can usually be built against it. That takes more work and needs looking after, so it's worth it for tools the team uses every day.

faq.q: Do we need a developer to use MCP?
faq.a: Not always. Ready connectors can often be switched on from the assistant's settings. Outside help earns its place in choosing permissions, testing, and building connectors for tools that don't have one.

title: Claude Setup for Teams: Working From the Firm's Own Data
h1: How to set up Claude for a team so it works from the firm's own data
desc: Setting up Claude for a team means a shared workspace, projects that hold the firm's context, connections to its tools, reusable instructions and training.
lead: Buying seats is the easy part of setting up Claude for a team. A useful setup adds a shared workspace, projects that hold the firm's own context, connections to the tools where its data lives, written instructions for the tasks it repeats every week, and training so each person knows what to ask.
short: Begin with a shared workspace and one project per area of work, holding the firm's own documents.
Connect the assistant to the tools the team copies from most, so it reads live records instead of pasted text.
Write reusable instructions for weekly tasks, so the same job comes out the same way whoever asks.
Train the team on its real tasks, and give each routine a named owner inside the firm.

sections.h2: What does a Claude setup for a team include?
body: Sign a team up, let everyone start typing, and they get a capable assistant that knows nothing about the firm. Every conversation starts from zero. Each person explains the same background again, and then again next week.
Setup is the work of giving the assistant that background once, so the team can spend its time on the task itself. A complete setup covers these parts:
A shared workspace, where the team's accounts, settings and access are managed in one place.
Projects that hold the firm's context: how it writes, what it offers, its templates and reference documents.
Connections to the tools where the firm's data lives, such as email, calendar, shared drive and the main database.
Reusable instructions for the tasks the team repeats every week.
Training and ownership, so people actually use it and someone keeps it current.

sections.h2: How should the workspace and projects be organised?
body: The workspace is the firm's account. It decides who has access, which features are on and which connections are allowed. One person should set it up, ideally someone who knows what data the firm is comfortable sharing with an assistant.

Projects are where most of the value sits. A project groups conversations around one area of work and keeps the documents and instructions the assistant should always have to hand. A firm might have one for client proposals, one for recruiting, one for marketing content and one for internal reporting.

Fill each project with the firm's own material. Past proposals that won work. The house style for reports. The description of services and the standard terms. Open the project and the assistant already knows how the firm writes and what it sells, so nobody pastes that in again.

Keep projects few and clearly named at first. A team that opens the assistant and sees a short list matching its real areas of work knows where to begin. Old drafts and personal experiments belong in personal space.

sections.h2: Which connections should come first?
body: Once the assistant can reach the firm's records directly, it gets a lot more useful. Claude connects to other tools through MCP, the Model Context Protocol, an open standard Anthropic introduced in November 2024. Many common tools already have a ready connector.

Pick the tool the team copies from most. In a lot of firms that's email and calendar, then the shared drive, then the main client or candidate database. Every connection starts with read access. Draft access comes later, where a routine needs it, and a person approves anything before it's sent to a client.
If a tool has no ready connector, Loose Ends builds the integration against that tool's API, so the assistant can still work from its data.

sections.h2: How do reusable instructions work for weekly tasks?
body: Every team has its weekly repeats. The client update. The pipeline summary. The newsletter draft, and the meeting notes turned into actions. When each person asks for these in their own words, the results wander and someone has to correct the assistant every time.

A reusable instruction writes the task down once. It says what the task is for, which sources to use, what shape the result takes, what to check, and where someone has to sign off. Claude handles this through project instructions and saved skills, so a short request starts the task and the structure comes out the same each time.
Good instructions for a weekly task usually cover:
What the task is for, and who reads the result.
Where the information comes from, for example last week's calendar and the client folder.
The exact format, with a short example of a good result.
Anything the assistant must never fill in by itself, such as figures or dates it can't find.
The point where a person reviews the work before it goes anywhere.

sections.h2: How was this done for a journalist working in video?
body: Loose Ends set up the AI assistant of a journalist who works in video. It was built around his editorial week, not around the software's defaults.

The work began with how his week actually runs. Which tasks he repeats, the order he does them in, and where video production falls. Those tasks were then written down as instructions the assistant follows, and they now run the same way every time, with video production at the centre.

What carries over to other firms is the approach. The assistant was shaped to one person's working week, so he never had to bend his week around whatever the assistant did out of the box. The work was delivered in 2026.

sections.h2: How should a team be trained, and who owns the setup?
body: Train people on their own tasks. A general session on what AI can do is forgotten within days. A session where each person runs their own weekly report through the project, looks at the result and fixes the instruction tends to stick, because it saves them work that same week.

Every routine also needs a named owner inside the firm. That person keeps the project documents current, adjusts instructions when the work changes, and is usually the first to spot a connection that has stopped returning what it should. Without an owner, even a good setup drifts out of date.

Loose Ends delivers this as a build at one fixed price agreed in writing, then a handover with training and a named owner for every routine. Accounts and access belong to the firm. To see which weekly tasks would gain most from a setup like this, ask Loose Ends for the free one-page review of where the firm loses time. No call is needed.

faq.q: Is a Claude setup only for large firms?
faq.a: No. The same approach works for an independent professional and for an established firm. One person gets as much from projects and reusable instructions as a team does.

faq.q: Can Claude send emails for the team?
faq.a: With the right connection it can draft them. In a Loose Ends setup, a person reads and approves anything before it goes to a client.

faq.q: What is the difference between a project and a connection?
faq.a: A project holds context the assistant always has, like templates and house style. A connection lets it reach live records in another tool, like the inbox or the client database.

faq.q: How do we keep the setup up to date?
faq.a: Give each routine a named owner who updates its documents and instructions when the work changes. Optional monthly support is there if the firm would rather have outside help.

title: AI Assistant Adoption Gap: Why Teams Use So Little of It
h1: Why most teams use a fraction of what their AI assistant can do, and how to close the gap
desc: Most teams use a fraction of their AI assistant because of the blank page, no access to the firm's data, no shared instructions and no owner. Each has a fix.
lead: Most teams use a fraction of what their AI assistant can do because it was switched on and never set up. The causes repeat from firm to firm: the blank page, no access to the firm's own data, no shared instructions for repeated tasks, and nobody owning the setup. Each one has a practical fix.
short: The gap rarely comes from the assistant's ability. It comes from how the assistant was introduced to the team.
The same causes come up again and again: the blank page, no access to the firm's data, no shared instructions, no owner.
Each has a fix: ready starting tasks, connections, written instructions and a named owner.
A person still approves anything the assistant prepares before it goes to a client.

sections.h2: What is the AI assistant adoption gap?
body: It's the distance between what an AI assistant could do for a firm and what the team actually uses it for. In plenty of firms the licences are paid and the assistant sits open in a browser tab. Now and then someone asks it to rephrase an email or summarise a document.

Meanwhile the chores that eat real time carry on by hand. Answering routine enquiries. Confirming bookings. Chasing unpaid invoices, retyping details from one tool into the next, filing documents. The assistant could prepare much of that work, but nobody has shown it how.
Closing this gap is the main offer at Loose Ends. The causes are predictable, and so are the fixes.

Ability is rarely the problem, and neither is the team's willingness. The trouble is how the assistant arrived. It was handed over as an empty box, with no link to the firm's records, no agreed way of doing the common tasks and nobody responsible for making it work. Each of those can be fixed separately, and the fixes add up.

sections.h2: Why does the blank page stop people?
body: An empty chat box expects the user to know what to ask and how to phrase it. Most people are busy and have a task in front of them, with no prompt in mind. So they ask for something small, get an average result, and decide the tool is only good for small things.
Stop starting from blank. For each role, write down the tasks that person repeats and turn them into ready starting points:
Named tasks per role, such as the Monday client update or the weekly pipeline summary.
A saved instruction for each task, which the person starts with a short request.
An example of a good finished result, so the assistant knows what to aim for.
A short note on what to check before using the result.
If the first proper use saves time on an actual task, people come back to it.

sections.h2: Why does no access to the firm's data matter so much?
body: An assistant that can't see the firm's records can only work with what gets pasted in. So every useful request starts with someone opening another tool, finding the right text, copying it and pasting it. That copying is often the exact chore the team hoped to get rid of.

Connections fix this. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard Anthropic introduced in November 2024. Through it, an assistant such as Claude can reach email, calendar, shared drives, team chat and business databases directly. When a tool has no ready connector, an integration can be built against its API.

Each connection should begin with read access, with draft access added where a routine needs it. What the firm ends up with is an assistant that answers from its own records, at the moment someone asks.

sections.h2: What goes wrong without shared instructions?
body: If every person writes their own request for the same task, the firm gets as many versions of that task as it has people. Reports come back in different shapes. One person remembers to check the figures and another doesn't. When someone leaves, their way of asking walks out with them.

Shared instructions turn a task into a routine. They're written once and kept where the whole team can reach them. Each one covers the goal, the sources, the format, what must never be guessed, and where a person signs off. Claude supports this with projects that hold the firm's context and reusable instructions.
Written instructions also make quality visible. When a result is wrong, the team fixes the instruction and every later run improves. Nobody is sitting on a private trick.

Put the approval step in the instruction itself. A weekly client update prepared by the assistant is a draft until someone has read it, checked it against the record and sent it. Once that step is written down, it doesn't get skipped on a busy Friday.

sections.h2: Why does the setup need an owner?
body: Tools that belong to everyone end up belonging to no one. Without an owner, the documents in the assistant's projects go stale. Connections break and nobody notices. Instructions describe how the work was done last year.
The owner doesn't need to be technical. The job is keeping the setup in step with the work:
Update reference documents when services, prices or templates change.
Adjust an instruction when the team reports a poor result.
Spot a connection that has stopped returning what it should, and get it fixed.
Walk new team members through the routines they'll use.
That's why Loose Ends hands over every routine with a named owner inside the firm.

sections.h2: How does a firm close the gap in practice?
body: Order matters. Train people before the assistant can reach the firm's data and they learn to paste. Write instructions before choosing the tasks and nobody uses them. A sounder order is to find the chores that cost the most time, connect the tools those chores depend on, write the instructions, and then train the team on those exact tasks.

The studio works in that order. It starts with a free one-page review of where the firm loses time, then a paid audit that ranks the first fixes, with the fee credited toward the build. The build is done at one fixed price agreed in writing. Handover includes training and a named owner for every routine, and the code, domain and accounts belong to the firm.

The design rule holds the whole way through. The assistant drafts and prepares, and people decide what goes out. The first step is that free one-page review of where the firm loses time, and it needs no call.

faq.q: Is the gap caused by people resisting AI?
faq.a: Usually not. Most teams stick to small tasks because the assistant was switched on with no access to the firm's data and no ready starting points. Once it saves time on an actual task, people use it.

faq.q: Does closing the gap mean the assistant acts on its own?
faq.a: No. It prepares drafts, summaries and documents, and a person approves anything before it's sent to a client.

faq.q: Which cause should a firm fix first?
faq.a: Usually access to the firm's data. Without it, the other fixes still leave the team copying and pasting. Then come shared instructions, training and an owner.

faq.q: Does this apply only to Claude?
faq.a: The causes are the same with any AI assistant. Loose Ends sets up Claude and other assistants, connected to the firm's own data.

title: Connect Claude to a Recruiting Database Such as Loxo
h1: How to connect an AI assistant to a recruiting database such as Loxo
desc: Connecting Claude to a recruiting database such as Loxo lets a search firm's team question its own candidate data in plain language, with access controlled.
lead: Connect an AI assistant such as Claude to a recruiting database such as Loxo, and a search firm's team can ask questions of its own candidate and role data in plain language. Nobody has to build searches by hand or export lists. The link runs through a connector or an integration with the database's API, with access limited to what the team needs and a person approving anything sent to a candidate or client.
short: A connected assistant answers from the firm's own candidate and role records.
The connection runs through MCP or through an integration built against the recruiting system's API.
Start with read access, and decide in writing which fields the assistant may see.
An executive search firm in Washington D.C. uses this setup, alongside open roles that flow from Loxo to its website.

sections.h2: What does connecting an assistant to a recruiting database do?
body: A search firm's memory lives in its recruiting database. Candidates and their history, notes from calls, roles open and closed, who was presented where. Getting an answer out of it usually means building a search, exporting a list, or asking the colleague who remembers.
With the assistant connected, the team asks in plain language. Questions like these:
Which candidates have been placed or presented for similar roles before?
What do the call notes say about this candidate's interest in moving?
Which open roles haven't had a new candidate added lately?
Summarise the history of this client's searches with the firm.
Draft a shortlist note from these candidates' records, for a consultant to review.
Answers come from the firm's records, and the assistant can point to the record it used so the consultant can check.

sections.h2: How does the connection work technically?
body: There are two routes. The first is MCP, the Model Context Protocol, an open standard Anthropic introduced in November 2024 for connecting AI assistants to tools and data. If a connector exists for the recruiting system, it can be switched on and given the right permissions.

The second route is for when no ready connector fits. An integration is built against the recruiting system's own API, the interface it offers other software. Loose Ends builds these and presents them to the assistant as a connector, so the team sees the same thing either way. A question goes into the chat, and the answer comes from the database.

In both cases the connector decides which actions the assistant can take, such as searching candidates, reading a record or reading notes. It passes each request to the database with the permissions it was given.

The whole database never lands in the chat. The assistant fetches the records it needs for the question in front of it, and the answer can show which ones it used. That keeps answers checkable. It also keeps the database as the one place where candidate information is stored and corrected.

sections.h2: What permissions should a search firm set?
body: Candidate data is personal data, and a search firm holds it in trust. Before connecting anything, decide what the assistant may see and do, and write it down.
A careful starting point:
Read access only at first. The assistant searches and reads. It doesn't edit or delete records.
A clear decision on which fields are included, and which sensitive ones stay out.
Access limited to team members who already have access to the database.
Messages to candidates or clients drafted only, with a consultant approving each one before it's sent.
A named owner who reviews the connection when the database or the team changes.
It's also worth checking that the firm's use of the assistant fits its own data policies and the terms it gives candidates.

sections.h2: How was this set up for an executive search firm in Washington D.C.?
body: Loose Ends works with an executive search firm in Washington D.C. that runs its searches in Loxo. The work connects the recruiting system to the firm's other tools, so information gets entered once.

Open roles go into Loxo and appear on the firm's eighteen-page website without anyone retyping them. Candidate CVs are put into the firm's format in one step. And the same database answers the team's questions through their AI assistant. Both the recruiting database and the firm's internal chat are connected to it, so a consultant can ask a question and get an answer from the firm's records.
The website is live. Candidate scoring is in development.

sections.h2: Where does candidate assessment fit?
body: Once the database is connected, candidates can also be assessed against a search's own criteria. Loose Ends has built assessment that scores against the criteria set for that search and puts the reasoning beside the score. A consultant sees why a candidate scored as they did, as well as how high.

Vero, the studio's own recruiting software, works on the same principle. It reads a batch of résumés against a role, ranks the candidates, and shows the reasoning and source text behind every score. It also drafts outreach from each candidate's own work. The decision stays with the recruiter.
In every case the system prepares and explains. The consultant decides.

sections.h2: What should a firm prepare before connecting?
body: Answers are only as good as the records behind them. Before connecting, find out which fields the team fills in reliably and which are often empty. Then nobody asks the assistant to answer from data that isn't there.
Collect the questions the team asks most in an ordinary week, too. They become the test set. The connection is ready when it answers them correctly and points to the right records.

Last, work out where the assistant fits in the team's day. A search firm that already talks in an internal chat tool can connect that chat as well. Consultants then ask questions where they already work, instead of opening yet another window. Training covers the firm's own questions, what the assistant can see, and what still needs a consultant's judgement.

Loose Ends builds this at one fixed price agreed in writing, with training and a named owner at handover, and the code and accounts belong to the firm. To see where a connected database would save the team the most retyping and searching, ask for the free one-page review of where the firm loses time. No call is needed.

faq.q: Can Claude connect to Loxo?
faq.a: Yes. Loose Ends has connected an executive search firm's Loxo database to its AI assistant, through an integration with Loxo's API that the assistant uses as a connector.

faq.q: Will the assistant change or delete candidate records?
faq.a: Not with read access only, which is the recommended start. Write access can be added later for specific routines the firm has approved.

faq.q: Can the assistant contact candidates directly?
faq.a: In a Loose Ends setup it only drafts messages. A consultant reads and approves each one before it's sent.

faq.q: Does this work with recruiting systems other than Loxo?
faq.a: The approach is the same for any recruiting system that has a connector or an API. Fields, permissions and tests are set up for each one.

title: Custom API Integration When No Connector Exists
h1: What to do when a tool has no ready connector: a custom API integration
desc: When a tool has no ready connector, a custom integration can be built against its API. What that involves, the risks, the upkeep, and who owns the result.
lead: When a tool a firm depends on has no ready connector for its AI assistant or its other software, the usual answer is a custom integration built against the tool's own API. Building one means reading the tool's documentation, deciding exactly what data moves and who can act on it, building and testing the link, and agreeing who looks after it and owns it afterwards.
short: An API is the interface a tool offers other software. Most business tools have one.
A custom integration talks to that API, and it can be exposed to an assistant such as Claude as an MCP connector.
The main risks are access that's too wide, changes to the tool's API, and nobody owning the result.
The firm should own the code and the accounts, including the API keys.

sections.h2: What does it mean when a tool has no connector?
body: A connector is a ready-made link between two pieces of software. For AI assistants, connectors usually follow MCP, the Model Context Protocol, an open standard Anthropic introduced in November 2024. Popular tools like email, calendars and shared drives often have one.

Plenty of the tools firms rely on don't. A specialist industry database, a booking system, a client portal, an older internal tool. The team covers the gap by hand, exporting, copying, retyping and filing. The tool might be central to the work and still sit outside every automation and out of the assistant's reach.
If it has an API, that gap can usually be closed with a custom integration.

sections.h2: What is an API, and how does a custom integration use it?
body: API stands for application programming interface. It's the door a tool provides for other software. A program sends a request, such as list open roles or create a booking, and the tool answers in a structured format, with nobody clicking through screens.

A custom integration is a small program that talks to that API for the firm. It can move data between tools on a schedule or whenever something changes. It can also be wrapped as an MCP connector so an assistant such as Claude can use it directly. Loose Ends builds them that way, so one piece of work serves both the automations and the assistant.

Most APIs want a key or a sign-in that identifies who's asking. Treat that key like a password. Create it under an account the firm controls, store it securely, and give it only the access the integration needs. If the firm parts ways with the builder, it can replace the key and keep the integration.

sections.h2: What does building a custom integration involve?
body: Most of the work is decisions. The code comes after them. A sound build goes through these steps:
Read the tool's API documentation to see what it allows, what it limits and how sign-in works.
Agree exactly which data moves, in which direction, and what must never be touched.
Pick the narrowest access that does the job, starting with read access where possible.
Build the integration and test it on a copy or a small set of real records.
Add a review step wherever the result reaches a client, so a person approves it first.
Write down how it works, where it runs and who to contact if it stops.

Here's a typical case. A firm enters open roles in its recruiting system, and an integration places them on its website, so nobody retypes them. Loose Ends built this for an executive search firm in Washington D.C. Open roles go into Loxo and appear on the firm's website, and the same database answers the team's questions through its AI assistant.

sections.h2: What are the risks of a custom integration?
body: A custom integration is real software and comes with real responsibilities. The risks are predictable, though:
Access that's too wide. An integration that can write to every record can damage every record if something goes wrong.
Changes to the API. The tool's maker can change or retire parts of it, and the integration has to keep up.
Silent failure. If an integration stops and nobody's told, the team assumes work is happening when it isn't.
Personal data. Moving client or candidate data between tools has to respect the firm's data policies and the tool's terms of use.
Dependence on one builder. If only the original builder understands it, the firm is exposed when that relationship changes.
Each has a plain answer. Narrow permissions. A check that reports failures to a named person. Written documentation. Code the firm owns.

Testing needs its own attention. Try the integration on ordinary records, on records with missing or odd fields, and on the case where the tool doesn't answer at all. Decide in advance what happens each time, whether that's skip and report, retry later, or stop and alert the owner. When the data reaches a client, a quiet guess is never acceptable.

sections.h2: Who maintains the integration, and who owns it?
body: An integration needs looking after for as long as it's in use. Someone has to notice when it fails, update it when the tool changes its API, and adjust it when the firm changes how it works. Agree who that is before the build starts. Finding out afterwards is how integrations get abandoned.

With Loose Ends, the code, domain and accounts belong to the firm, including the API keys and the account the integration runs under. At handover the integration has a named owner inside the firm and written notes on how it works. From there the firm can maintain it itself, hand it to another developer, or take optional monthly support from the studio.

sections.h2: When is a custom integration worth building?
body: Not every gap justifies one. It pays off when a tool is used every day, when the team copies from it often, and when mistakes in that copying cost the firm something. A tool opened once a month is usually better handled by hand or with an export.
Check first whether a ready connector, an official plug-in or a built-in export already covers the need. Build custom only when none of those exist or none of them reach the data the team needs.

Loose Ends builds integrations at one fixed price agreed in writing, after a paid audit that ranks the first fixes, with the audit fee credited toward the build. The first step is the free one-page review of where the firm loses time, and it needs no call.

faq.q: Can any tool be connected to an AI assistant?
faq.a: Most tools with an API can. A tool with no API and no export is much harder to connect reliably, and the honest answer may be to keep that step manual.

faq.q: Is a custom integration the same as an MCP connector?
faq.a: Not always. The integration is the link to the tool's API. It can be wrapped as an MCP connector for an assistant such as Claude, or run on its own to move data between tools.

faq.q: What happens when the tool changes its API?
faq.a: The integration has to be updated. With a check that reports failures to a named owner, the change gets noticed quickly, before weeks of data go missing.

faq.q: Who owns the integration after it is built?
faq.a: With Loose Ends, the firm owns the code, domain and accounts. It can maintain the integration itself, pass it to another developer, or take optional monthly support.
